content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper provides a method of selecting the optimal set of covariates when a causal graph is unknown, and the underlying unknown graph is Markovian. Based on Theorem 1, the proposed method recasts the problem into combinatorial optimization, and an RL-based method is leveraged to identify the optimal subset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength
1. This paper contains an interesting result in Theorem 1.

## Weakness
1. I think this paper can be written more clearly. A current paper contains many redundant discussions. 
2. Some theoretic results can be debated (Lemma 3.1.)
3. No formal learning guarantees are provided (in Section 4).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Clearity

1. I think the problem should be more explicitly written. In particular, I think the underlying assumption of the paper (e.g., no causal graphs are assumed) must be clearly described; otherwise, readers will not see any difference with the paper of Rotnitzky and Smucler. 
2. Also, the assumption must be clearly written. Specifically, the paper relies on the assumption that there are no hidden confounders between variables (i.e., the underlying causal graph is Markovian). Without this assumption, the results of Rotnitzky and Smucler and this paper will not hold. 
3. There are many redundant information in the paper. First, the paper contains many unrelated and improper citations, and little attention is taken to the most relevant paper. For example, how is this paper related with Wu & Fukumizu (2021); Zou (2022); Karimi et al., (2020)? Also, I think more reviews for the most relevant paper, Rotnitzky and Smucler (2020), must be written in Introduction section. Second, some paragraphs like Section 2.1 seems irrelevant to the paper. 
4. I don’t know why authors leveraged an RL-based method for the optimization. It seemed that the optimization problem can be solved through a simple greedy search, based on the result in Theorem 1. Why on earth readers want to leverage complicated deep-RL based method for solving a relatively simple optimization problem? 
5. Also, a theoretic learning gurantee for the proposed RL-based optimization is missing. Can the proposed method find the global optimizer? Otherwise, how accurate the method can be? It’s unclear how the discussion in Section 4 is related to solving the optimization problem accurately. 

## Novelty

1. Authors claimed that the paper is novel because it considered the case where the variables {I, X, Z} are correlated. However, given that the graph must be Markovian, it must be the case where the correlations are induced by causation (either I → X or X → I; and Z → X or X → Z). In other words, the correlation induced by hidden confounders between I, X, Z are not allowed because of the imposed Markovian setting. Therefore, I think the paper doesn’t fullly generalize the problem, as it claimed in the 3rd paragraph of the introduction. 

## Questions

1. In Eqs. (2,3), I think it must be Y, instead of Y(t) or Y(T). 
2. I disagree with the sentence “(b) they utilize the original expression of efficient influence curve, namely $D^{eff}$, to derive the asymptotic variance, which is not computationally tractable.” In deriving the asymptotic variance, $\gamma(P)$ is treated as a constant. Therefore, the first three terms in the rhs of Eq. (2) are sufficient for computing the asymptotic variance. Therefore, I don’t understand why we need Lemma 3.1.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, I think the paper can be written more clearly. In particular,

1. problems need to be defined clearly.
2. Assumptions should be posited explicitly.
3. Redundant discussions in the paper should be excluded.
4. Learning guarantees for RL-based optimization should be provided.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.title: reply to reviewer tc6m
content.comment:
## Thanks for your review

1.  We will clarify our assumptions and explanations more clearly.

2.  How such a combinational optimization can be achieved in a greedy approach? There is no existing theoretical guarantee that one greedy search can achieve near-optimal appxoimation for this NP hard problem. Moreover, we perform time test in our experimental parts, to show that the exhaustive search is exponential and impossible. In fact, google brain first develop the RL-based framework for combinational optimization, and HUAWEI has win the best paper in 2019 using this framework for causal discovery.


3. Unfortunately, no guarantee is available for the above-mentioned RL-based combination optimization framework. And we think it is independent work. 

4. We feel sorry to forget to claim the core assumption that no mediation variables exist due to time reasons, and we will add this assumption during revision.

5. We cannot agree with your claims in Question (2). The efficient influence curve in equ (2) has an underlying parameter, $\gamma(P)$. And our variance expression is the expectation w.r.t the quadratic of the efficient influence curve. How can you compare different variances induced by different adjustment features? In other words, which one in $\{(\gamma(P)+A)^2,(\gamma(P)+B)^2\}$ is larger? If you take $\gamma(P)$ as a constant, you can only compare among expectations rather than the variance (which one in  $\{(\gamma(P)+A),(\gamma(P)+B)\}$ is larger).

6. Our paper is not relevant to Wu & Fukumizu (2021), Karimi et al., (2020). The former studies on using VAE for ITE estimation, while our paper aims to separate adjustment variables for ATE. The latter studies on feasible algorithmic recourse for model explanation, which is totally uncorrelated to our problem.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper provides a metric Optimal Adjustment Features (OAF) to find an optimal adjustment set for average causal effect estimation from observational data. The proposed OAF metric is to minimize the variance of adjustment features. The theoretical analysis shows that the proposed OAF achieves an optimal selection of adjustment features. A reinforcement learning approach is used to search for the corresponding optimal adjustment set. The experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show the performance of the proposed method in comparison with some baseline methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
S1 The paper proposes an OAF metric for searching for optimal adjustment features.
S2 A reinforcement learning framework, OAFP, is developed for optimizing OAF and generating the corresponding feature mask for selecting adjustment features.


W: There is a gap between the method and the objective.

The data is generated from a causal graph with post treatment and post outcome variables. For such a causal graph, ATE may not be able to be estimated from data with the backdoor adjustment. So the method misses one step to ensure that the causal effect is identifiable in the data.  If the causal effect is not identifiable, the algorithm is misleading. For example, how do the authors distinguish the following two cases (1) $T \leftarrow X_1 \to Y$ . (2) $T \to X_1 \to Y$? In the second case, the cause effect cannot be estimated by the back door adjustment.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Good. The paper is well organised, and easy to follow.
Quality: Incomplete work.
Novelty: Low. The impact is low.
Reproducibility: Most details are provided for reproducibility.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims at identifying a set of optimal adjustment variables for unbiased causal effect estimation. A new metric proposed for the optimal adjustment set, and a reinforcement learning approach is said to be used to search for the optimal set. Experiments are conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The topic studied by the paper (causal effect estimation) is important and challenging.

Weakness:
1. Low quality of presentation. There are many English errors, confusing statements/understanding and technical errors in the paper, such that it is very hard to understand the authors' ideas and recognize the quality of the work. 
2. The goal of the paper is unclear. It's not sure whether the proposed method is for adjustment set discovery, average causal effect estimation or conditional causal effect estimation.
3. The motivation or problem setting of the paper is unclear and likely to be wrong. From Figure 1(c) and the relevant description, it seems that the paper may consider including descendants of treatment and/or outcome variables in the adjustment set for confounding control, which is incorrect.
4. It's hard to judge the novelty or correctness of the proposed metric, as there is not a clear explanation of the context or the meaning of metric, and the notation is confusing too, e.g. it's unclear what I(.) stands for in Eqn. (2) or Eqn. (3).
5. The reinforcement learning method is not well explained, making it difficult to understand or appreciate it.
6. The experiment evaluation part has many doubts. For example, it seems that some of the baselines (e.g. IPW) is for ATE estimation and some are for ITE/CATE estimation, so not sure what the comparison with the baseline is for; if the proposed method is for adjustment set discovery, then the discovered adjustment set (the variables in the set) should have been reported/discussed; the results in Table 3 - the best results are wrongly highlighted, e.g. with IHDP, basedline DVD has the best performance, and with Twins, baselines DragonNet and BART both outperforms the proposed method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper tries to tackle an important and interesting problem. However, unfortunately the low presentation quality makes it impossible to properly understand the work, and there are issues with the technical quality too at described above.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the problem studied by the paper is important, the quality of the paper is low overall.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors present a reinforcement learning-based framework for determining optimal adjustment sets and propose a new metric for evaluating the quality of adjustment set. The authors show that the metric should be minimised iff the adjustment features contain confounders and outcome variables only and show that the proposed method works to achieve precise treatment effect estimation on synthetic data sets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The problem examined in this paper is an especially important and interesting one and would be very useful to solve in practice. The paper also uses multiple data sets in the experiments section to substantiate some of its claims. The authors also try to present some discussion about the theoretical properties of the proposed metric to further support their claims.

However, the paper has a lot of points that need clarifying and further details and several important baselines are missing. The experiments section is especially confusing. Together this issues make it hard to justify some of the claims. Below I detail some of these points:

1) First, the authors need to make their assumptions clear throughout. Are the authors assuming unconfoundedness? If dealing with the sequential setting as implied by the need for a reinforcement learning based framework, does this require any form of sequential ignorability? Why or why not?

2) Covariate separation has been proposed by several works (incl Hassanpour et al 2019) and other approaches using deep generative models such as VAEs that learn separate subspaces for adjustment of treatment and outcomes. The authors only mention some of this work and are missing several related pieces.

3) In Figure 1 c, the authors introduce linked edges between I, X, Z, T and Y to illustrate that correlations between X and I and Z are allowed but dont describe what allowing this correlation enables and why its necessary or important in this case. More crucially though, the figure in Figure 1 c is no longer a causal DAG so how is treatment effect estimation performed on this? Please be specific about the causal assumptions and the causal DAG you are dealing with.

4) Perhaps the most confusing aspect of the paper is the use of the proposed reinforcement learning framework. Reinforcement learning is typically applied in a sequential decision making context. Though there are many works that make explicit the role of causality in reinforcement learning, each of these considers sequential decisions. Yet the authors never test the proposed approach on a sequential decision making task, but rather use the synthetic IHDP and Twins datasets to construct some type of pre-treatment/post-treatment setup. Though the performance seems good, the setup seems very contrived and I'm not convinced by it. I would like to see a real world experiment with a specific example of how the proposed framework is applied in a sequential setting where the authors are clear about what are the states, actions and rewards and what the sequential decision making problem is and how using the proposed framework works in comparison to just learning a vanilla say MDP that does not perform adjustment to reason about treatment effects and a suitable policy.

5) The authors also need to justify how they define optimality of adjustment sets here. Many adjustment sets may be found. Can you guarantee in some way that none of these provide over/under adjustment of variables? Moreover, are these adjustment sets unique? If not, then there may be multiple such plausible sets so how can we be sure about this? Can we characterise broadly what optimal adjustment should entail
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The work is not clear and though some of the details are there, it is very difficult to grasp significance of the contribution when the experiments and setup are so unclear.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think the paper tries to address an important problem but does a poor job at explaining clearly how to go about doing so and lacks experimental backing.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: reply to reviewer prn8
content.comment:
## Thanks for your review

1. For vague issues in our paper, we will clarify them more clearly.

2. This paper has claimed the unconfoundness assumption and deals with the static causal inference. Hence  sequential ignorability is no not required. 

3. We allow X and Z to be post-treatment and post-outcome, and also correlations between them, except for the mediation variables. 

4. I think our reforcement learning framework does not concerned with sequential learning. Google brain has developed this framework to efficiently perform combinational optimiation. We will clarify this part more clearly.

5. The characterization of the optimality is not clear in our paper. We will clarify this more clearly. Our main theorem has claimed this with remark. We might put these explanations in more significant places in our paper.
